title: This tree: same one-session gap as dropssh B1; carry the proxy-aware ws + env-token forward; answer to issue 2 is 'no new repo, implement the multiplexer once in dropssh'
body:
# This tree: same one-session gap, and three things it already has that dropssh's backlog wants

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a decision to
build.**

**Provenance.** this tree at commit `6b561f659870`, read 2026-08 (cloned and
read 2026-09-28). Read `AGENTS.md`, `README.md`, and the source at
`bin/sandssh` and `relay/sandssh-relay.py`. ⛔ Checked against **source**, not
against `AGENTS.md`, which is itself a claim.

## The gap, confirmed in source

`bin/sandssh:738-780` (`cmd_serve`) is one-session-per-connection, the same
shape as dropssh B1:

```python
log("client paired; session open")
pipe_sock_to_proc(io, server_cmd)      # serves ONE session
log("session ended; redialing in %ss" % backoff)
time.sleep(backoff); backoff = min(backoff*2, 30)
```

So the **python** transport pairs, serves one ssh session, tears down, redials.
**Neither this tree nor dropssh implements the multiplexed reverse path.**
`AGENTS.md` is right that there is no client-side relay verb (the relay is
`relay/sandssh-relay.py`, a separate stdlib process) and right that the C
`dropssh` is the more capable of the two.

## What this tree already has, that the reverse-multiplexing work wants

Three things, found by reading the source, that are **not** in dropssh's
backlog as written:

1. ⛔ **A proxy-aware websocket client in the tree.** `cmd_serve`/`cmd_connect`
   use `ws_connect(url, "/v1/node/%s", ..., proxy=PROXY, verify=not
   args.insecure)` and `raw_dial(url)`. This matters because this sweep
   **measured** that a cage's only egress is an HTTP CONNECT proxy and that
   `net.connect`/`tls.connect` bypass it. The python tree already routes
   through `PROXY`; dropssh's equivalent is `transport.c`'s HTTP CONNECT. Both
   are load-bearing and both belong in the **doctor** (dropssh R3).
2. ⛔ **A `--transport ws` mode with `/v1/node/` and `/v1/connect/`.** The
   same reverse-relay URL shape and the same `hello`/`ready` framing the PoC
   proved live. ⛔ The two trees are already converging on one protocol; the
   multiplexer only has to be written once.
3. ⚠ **`SANDSSH_RELAY_KEY` from the environment.** dropssh's **R5 pair** idea,
   half-built. ⛔ It also has `--insecure`, a footgun dropssh correctly does
   not have. If anything is carried across it is the env-var token, **not** the
   flag.

## Verdict for this repository

Issue #2 asks that sandssh "become tool agnostic & redundant". ⛔ **The seven
tools do not change this repository's shape.** They change what goes *inside*
dropssh's reverse multiplexer, and this tree is the reference implementation
of the same node semantics in python. The right outcome: implement B1–B7 once,
in dropssh (C), and keep this tree as the interop reference that `podbox`'s
tests exercise. ⛔ **No new repository.** That is the answer to the issue's
"or maybe a single tool" — the single tool already exists; the gap is inside
it.

## What the sweep adds to this tree's docs

* ⛔ **`docs/relay-issues.md` B11 is stale** (see the gap issue): a bare node
  frame now closes 1009, not silence — five places in dropssh's docs.
* ⛔ **`relay/DEPLOY.md`'s UDS form is confirmed** by websocat #255 (UDS still
  open upstream) and already exists in dropssh `transport.c`.

title: Measured: the cage constraints (no bind even at uid 0, no resolver, 443-only egress proxy) — the conditions every verdict rests on
body:
# Measured: the host and egress constraints every verdict rests on

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **These are the conditions,
not recommendations.** They are recorded separately because every other issue
in this sweep is conditional on them, and because the method requires a
write-up to open with what it did *not* establish.

One machine, one day: **Linux 6.18.54, uid 0, 2026-09-28**, gcc 14.2, go
1.27.1, rustc 1.98.1. Re-run the three scripts in the corpus to reproduce;
each prints its own conditions. This sandbox is a **sealed cage, and a
tighter one than the issue assumes**.

## What was measured

| probe | result | why it matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `bind(2)` TCP `127.0.0.1:0`, **at uid 0** | `bind: Permission denied` | the cage cannot bind **even as root**. Nothing can listen, not even a loopback SOCKS. Every "client-side listener" design (chisel forward, a local SOCKS, the Cloudflare recipe's listener leg) is dead here. |
| `/dev/ptmx` | absent | no pty. `script` (curlshell's TTY trick), Mosh-style local echo, any PTY spawn are dead. |
| `/etc/passwd` | absent | as documented for cages. |
| UDP `socket`+`bind` | **ok** | ⛔ do **not** assume "a cage has no UDP" on the basis of the docs; it is true for the target cage but **not measured here**. |
| resolver | `getent hosts example.com` → no answer; `getent` `EAI_AGAIN`; `/etc/resolv.conf` lists 1.1.1.1 but queries do not resolve | no working DNS. By-IP works (`https://1.1.1.1/` → 301). |
| direct TCP:443 (openssl, `net.connect`, `tls.connect`) | **all time out** | all TLS egress is via the CONNECT proxy at `169.254.169.1:44099` (`NODE_USE_ENV_PROXY=1` for node). A client that ignores the env proxy cannot reach anything. |
| non-443 CONNECT | **`403 not on the egress allowlist`**, 24/24 trials | only 443 is reachable. A public VPS on 8080, DoH on 853, and ssh on 22 are all refused. A Cloudflare worker (443) is survivable; a normal tunnel server is not. |

## The load-bearing result: the egress allowlist is port-443 only

`20-probe-the-egress.sh` observed 443 reached and 22/8080/9999/853 refused.
Because one refusal pattern decides the Cloudflare and websocat verdicts,
`30-confirm-connect-allowlist.sh` is the **control**: 4 hosts x 2 ports x 3
trials, printing the raw CONNECT reply, and the proxy names the policy itself.

```
example.com   443 | 200 Connection Established x3
github.com    443 | 200 Connection Established x3
cloudflare.com 443 | 200 Connection Established x3
1.1.1.1       443 | 200 Connection Established x3
example.com   22 | 403 not on the egress allowlist x3
… (all four hosts, 22) …
VERDICT: the restriction HELD. exit 0.
```

Mutation-proven: a script that rewrites the 403 into a 200 (simulating a
proxy with no restriction) exits **1**. Read **unpiped** — the first run was
piped and reported the pipe's exit code, which is the trap `dropssh/AGENTS.md`
warns about.

## ⛔ What this did NOT establish

* One machine, one day. A cage with wider egress or a real VPS may differ in
  both directions.
* ⛔ **The DNS experiments re-derive a solved problem.** `dropssh/src/dns.c`
  is already a three-source resolver (getaddrinfo → `/etc/hosts` → DoH over
  HTTPS) and its header records the *same* EAI_AGAIN measurement in the
  reference cage a day earlier. The corpus keeps those runs as a second-host
  **confirmation** and a re-runnable instrument, and offers them as **no new
  work**.
* ⛔ An earlier line claiming "DoH on 853 is refused, so dropssh's fallback is
  blocked" was **false** — dropssh resolves over HTTPS (443), which is
  permitted. Corrected in the corpus.

## Why it matters for the rest of the sweep

The host is bindless **even as root**, which is *stronger* than the issue's
premise and removes any mechanism whose first step is a local listener in the
cage (ligolo's tun is on the proxy, wiretap needs a WireGuard interface, a
cage-side SOCKS cannot bind, the Cloudflare listener leg is dead). It also
**proves this sandbox is a valid stand-in for the target cage**, which the
method's part (b) needs.

title: Reference: awesome-tunneling — confirms the maintainer's own 'no single tool exists'; refuses hosted tunnels (tracker: they die)
body:
# Reference: anderspitman/awesome-tunneling — confirms the "dream", refuses the dependencies

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a build
decision.**

**Provenance.** commit `a17321d82c27`, mined 2026-09-28 (route gh, control
reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker: 306 issues+PRs (both states), 520 comments, 6
review comments, 0 discussions. The "tree" is a `README.md` and a `scripts/`
dir. Three passes read. Cite this commit beside every line.

**What it is.** A curated list of ~150 tunneling tools. A **directory**, not a
mechanism — the maintainer says so: "to track and compare tunneling
solutions." No code to adopt.

**Its own "dream" is the most useful part**, because it is the maintainer
stating, in 2026, what is still missing after a decade of the category:
> "So far I haven't found a tool that does all of this… none of them integrate
> the domain registration and DNS management in a simple way."

The four wants: a domain auto-pointed at the tunnel, free automatic HTTPS,
"a client tool that tunnels through the server **without requiring root on the
client**", and a GUI. ⛔ That third one is the *easy* half of our problem:
our client is uid 0 and still cannot `bind(2)`. ⛔ **Read against our
constraints, the list's framing is optimistic about cage-shaped clients** —
which is why adopting a recommendation wholesale would be wrong.

## What to adopt
* ⛔ **Nothing as a mechanism** (no code). Its "Recommendations" point at
  Cloudflare Tunnel (closed, hosted), Pangolin/frp (need a VPS), and
  SirTunnel. All need a public server we would have to operate.
* ⭐ **Its tracker is the real artefact.** 306 issues / 520 comments are a
  longitudinal record of *which hosted tunnels died and why* — cost evidence no
  README gives, and the answer to "and many more" in the issue. Unambiguous:
  * #184 "Btunnel has stopped working (502)" (closed)
  * #119 "tunneller public host seems to be down" (closed)
  * #53, #211 — the **upstream project** 404'd (Inlets, Ockam)
  * #31 — README now says greenhouse.server.garden "is currently unavailable
    and the project appears unmaintained (last activity 2023)"
  * #191, #176, #107 (closed) — hosted-vs-open-source drift
  * #162 "Hey, don't trust Loophole" (closed) — a warning *in the tracker*
  * #107 asks whether hosted and open-source are the same thing. ⛔ The best
    single argument for our posture: **a dependency whose hosted and
    self-hosted forms differ can change under you.**
  * ⛔ **The finding: every tool in this category we would depend on has, at
    some point, been dead, moved, or relicensed.** The list's own 2026-02-16
    policy (require 100 GitHub stars) is itself a response to submissions
    that disappear.
* ⛔ **Lift the licence check.** The list records #6 (Tailscale → BSD-3 +
    PATENTS) and #25 (Inlets is not open source, closed): licences change, so
    any adopted mechanism must be licence-checked **at the commit we cite**.

## What NOT to adopt
* ⛔ **The "single tool that does it all" framing.** The maintainer's own
  answer is "I haven't found one" — that is a nine-year-old open problem. Our
  answer is narrower and built: one relay, one binary, one session.
* ⛔ **Hosted tunnels** (Cloudflare Tunnel, ngrok, zrok, tunnelto, bore.pub…).
  Each is a second operator, a second trust root, and a shutdown risk this
  tracker's own issues document. ⛔ Production quality is not the requirement;
  **continuing to exist next year** is, and the evidence says hosted tunnels in
  this category do not.
* ⛔ **WireGuard overlay tools** (`tunnel.pyjam.as` and the overlay section) —
  a TUN and privileged routing, which our cage cannot do. Independently,
  wiretap #61 reports WireGuard/UDP blocked in some jurisdictions.

## Tracker findings not about dead services
* #5, #123 (closed): users want client and server to be the *same* program
  and audit its language. ⛔ A mild, real argument for dropssh's "one binary,
  several verbs" shape.
* #88 (closed): ngrok's `go-update` hit an **expired x509** at startup. ⛔ A
  tool that phones home is a tool that stops working. **confirms** our
  "nothing at runtime" rule.
* #59 suggests `autossh`; #244 asks for any free TCP tunnel without a credit
  card; #184 shows a 502.

**Not settled:** whether any tool on the list would work in our cage. ⛔ None
were run. The verdict is structural (they need a public server, a TUN, a
domain, or a hosted service we do not operate), read from their own
descriptions, not from execution. A session that wants to overturn it should
run one, not read one more.

title: Reference: websocat/Cloudflare any-TCP — refuse (we have a 443 relay the cage reaches today); 4th project reporting the lifecycle/teardown class
body:
# Reference: vi/websocat + the iq.thc.org Cloudflare recipe — refuse, and document why

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a build
decision.**

**Provenance (websocat).** commit `3a3574cd2f5d`, mined 2026-09-28 (route
gh, control reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker: 309 issues+PRs, 1341 comments, 44
review comments, 0 discussions. Three passes read. Cite this commit beside
every line.

**Provenance (the THC recipe).** <https://iq.thc.org/tunnel-via-cloudflare-to-any-tcp-service>.
⛔ **Not archived and not read at fetch time** — a web page, not a repository.
Named as a gap. Nothing below depends on its contents; the verdict is derived
from the **measured host constraint**.

**What websocat is.** "Netcat, curl and socat for WebSockets" (its README): a
byte-stream bridge between a WebSocket and one of stdio / a file / a
subprocess (`exec:`, `sh-c:`, `cmd:`) / TCP (`TcpListenClass`) / unix socket.
Not a tunneler in the ngrok sense. The interesting part for us is
`exec:`/`sh-c:` — "a WebSocket in, a process's stdin/stdout" — which is the
shape of an ssh-over-websocket and what the Cloudflare recipe composes with a
worker.

## The verdict: refused, with the measured reason
The any-TCP-over-Cloudflare technique is a Worker that accepts a WebSocket,
opens a TCP socket to an arbitrary `host:port`, and splices. Read against what
our cage can do:

1. ⛔ **The cage is bindless.** `bind(2)` on `127.0.0.1:0` fails **at uid 0**
   (measured). The recipe's "local listener" variant is dead; the
   "client dials the worker" variant survives. Same wall every other
   reference hit.
2. ⚠ **Only 443 through the egress proxy.** Every non-443 CONNECT is
   `403 not on the egress allowlist` (24/24 trials); 443 is `200`. A worker is
   on 443, so this point is **survivable here** — recorded because it would
   kill the recipe in most cages and here it does not.
3. ⛔ **We already have a relay, and it is better than a public worker.** The
   ajam reverse relay is a first-party multiplexer on 443 a cage reaches
   **today** (proven live). A worker is a *second* public service between cage
   and operator — a second failure domain — for a capability (reach an
   arbitrary public TCP service) we do not need: the operator is already
   reachable, which is the actual job.
4. ⚠ **A worker is a deploy, an account, and a third party** the cage cannot
   provision. Cost measured in ongoing operational burden.

## What to adopt
* ⛔ **Nothing from websocat itself.** It is a debugging/bridging tool; our
  client is an ssh ProxyCommand. ⛔ **confirms** B4 with a second source: its
  help states that bridging a bytestream side to a message-oriented side
  "operates in lines" — the same message-vs-byte-stream discipline that makes
  dropssh's `ws_read` (B4) dangerous.
* ⚠ **A recipe, not a code path.** If a cage ever needs a public TCP service
  off our relay, the shape is "dial the worker on 443 through the CONNECT
  proxy, splice stdio". Recorded so the next session starts from the
  measurement, not from the THC page.

## What NOT to adopt
* ⛔ A Cloudflare worker in the path (second hop, second operator, second thing
  to page). ⛔ Reaching non-443 ports from the cage (hard wall here). ⛔
  websocat as a dependency (a Rust binary that must be present in a cage that
  takes one static C binary).

## Tracker findings the code does not say
* ⛔ **#35** "servermode eating a CPU core after closing TCP socket" and **#13**
  "Socket leak unless -E": a bridge tool leaks and spins on socket close. The
  **B7 (no backpressure/teardown)** class from a **fourth** project. Four
  independent projects in this corpus report the same class: *connection
  lifecycle and teardown*, not forwarding. ⛔ That is the strongest signal in
  the sweep and it should shape what is built first.
* **#99 "SSH through CDN", #102 "corporate proxy with auth"** (closed): users
  doing our job with websocat — the need is real, the tool is not the answer.
* **#37 (PROXY protocol), #262 (ALPN), #255 (UDS)** all open upstream. ⛔ UDS is
  the "relay in a bindless cage over a unix socket" shape `sandssh/relay/DEPLOY.md`
  already documents and dropssh's `transport.c` already has. **confirms.**

**Not settled:** whether a Cloudflare worker can open a TCP socket to an
arbitrary host. ⛔ Not tested — a question about Cloudflare's platform, not our
code. The verdict does not depend on it: we refuse the recipe because we
already have a better relay and the cage cannot deploy or bind, not because
the worker cannot splice.

title: Reference: sshx — refuse Redis mesh/web UI; adopt predictive echo + latency estimate; #18 is the E2E-auth lesson
body:
# Reference: ekzhang/sshx — refuse the transport, adopt 2 UX ideas

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a build
decision.**

**Provenance.** commit `3604e8ec5ce0`, mined 2026-09-28 (route gh, control
reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker: 153 issues+PRs, 354 comments, 35 review comments,
0 discussions. Three passes read. Cite this commit beside every line.

**The mechanism that decides the verdict: it is a UI, not a transport.** The
"globally distributed mesh" is Redis-backed —
`crates/sshx-server/src/state/mesh.rs:30`: "All servers must be accessible to
each other through TCP mesh networking"; `:49` a separate `redis::Client` for
pub/sub; `:165` `listen_for_transfers`. Plus a Rust client, a Rust server, and
a Svelte/xterm.js front end. We have one relay and no Redis; a browser leg is
a *presentation* of a byte stream, which `ssh -o ProxyCommand` already is.

## What to adopt
1. **Predictive echo, "a la Mosh"** (README feature list): local-echo with
   server reconciliation, so a 200 ms relay does not feel like 200 ms per
   keystroke. ⛔ Needs a pty on the far side, which a cage lacks — belongs in
   the client tty / `errandsh`, not the relay. Filed, not adopted here.
2. **Automatic reconnection with latency estimates** (README). ⛔
   **confirms** our property, stated better: the session is E2E-encrypted and
   the relay is a dumb pipe (our `AGENTS.md` says the same). ⛔ The
   **latency estimate** is the adoptable half — the same thing chisel prints
   (`Connected (Latency 204.880527ms)`, in #579's logs) and the same thing
   our **R3** (`doctor`) wants to report without guessing.

## What NOT to adopt
* ⛔ The mesh + Redis (a distributed fleet is the opposite of one relay; a new
  runtime dependency breaks "nothing to install").
* ⛔ The web terminal front end (Svelte, xterm.js, shared cursors). A product
  surface, not a capability. If a browser terminal is wanted later it is a new
  deliverable with its own issue.
* ⛔ `curl … | sh` self-install (same shape as curlshell: a bootstrap, not a
  transport, and it installs a third-party binary).

## Tracker findings the code does not say
* ⛔ **#12, #13 (closed) E2E encryption**, then **#18 (closed) "The commands are
  encrypted but not authenticated, allowing the server to tamper with them"**.
  A real, closed design lesson: encryption without authentication lets the
  relay tamper. We should be **authenticated** end to end — ssh already is
  (host key + pubkey). **confirms, with the reason.**
* ⛔ **#16, #144, #336, #372, #480, #615** all report AV flagging the binary
  or a corporate proxy blocking it. A single static binary with a reverse-TCP
  shape trips heuristic AV. ⛔ This is an operational tax on the *shape* of
  these tools and corroborates the house decision to keep **ssh** (a
  legitimate server) rather than a bespoke tunnel binary.
* **#31 (open)** "trusted certificates / CAs" is our **R7** (ship the CA
  bundle). **#74 (open)** "bypass certificate validation" is a footgun we
  refuse.
* **#49, #32** zombie process / memory leak / recovery on disconnect: again
  the **lifecycle** class, third project in a row.

**Not settled:** whether a browser terminal is wanted at all — a product
decision, out of scope for a transport research unit. Named, not answered.

title: Reference: curlshell — adopt curl|sh bootstrap idea (owner: sandhome); refuse the code (unlicensed clone, python, needs a 443 listener)
body:
# Reference: SkyperTHC/curlshell — adopt the bootstrap idea, refuse the code, owner is sandhome

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a build
decision.**

**Provenance.** commit `ed819e7bfa17`, mined 2026-09-28 (route gh, control
reachable, 0 gaps). **The whole tree is two files** — `curlshell.py` (9043
bytes) and `README.md`. ⛔ **No licence file**, and `README.md:3` says
"(Cloned from …/irsl/curlshell; slightly enhanced)". The tracker is empty (0
issues, 0 comments, 0 reviews, 0 discussions). There is nothing to read but
the script. ⛔ **Cite, do not copy** — no licence means nothing may be pasted
into `sandssh`.

**What it is.** An encrypted reverse shell: operator runs a TLS listener, the
target runs `curl -skfL https://operator:8080 | sh`. Its own framing: "The
target only needs `curl` and `sh`. Python is not needed." It works through a
SOCKS or HTTP proxy. It is the **only** thing in the seven that runs in a
proxy-only cage — which is why it is worth reading and why the verdict is
nuanced.

## Why it is not a transport
1. ⛔ **A reverse shell, not an ssh session.** No host key, no pubkey, no
   authenticated stream (sshx's #18 is the cautionary case: encrypted but
   not authenticated lets the server tamper). We have pubkey + host key;
   curlshell replaces that with a URL.
2. ⛔ **It needs a listener the cage can reach.** The target curls
   `https://1.2.3.4:8080`. Our egress answers `403 not on the egress
   allowlist` on every non-443 port (24/24 trials), so the operator would
   need a public **443** listener — a deployed service, not a `curl | sh`.
3. ⛔ **It is python.** A `socketserver`/`ssl` listener. The transport is one
   static C binary; a python listener on the operator's machine is tolerable,
   a python client in the cage is not, and this has no client at all.
4. ⚠ **The TTY trick cannot survive a cage.** `script -qc '/bin/bash -il'`
   needs a pty; our cage has **no `/dev/ptmx`** (measured).

## What to adopt (the idea, in our words, in another repo)
**Delivery as one `curl | sh` through the 443 proxy**: a cage reachable only
via a proxy can still be given an agent with nothing written to disk and no
binary installed. ⛔ This is a **bootstrap** path (sandhome), not a second
transport. Two requirements its README gets right and a naive bootstrap
misses: it must **honour the proxy** (our host: only a proxy-aware client can
fetch; a direct fetch times out) and it must need **only `curl` and `sh`** on
the target (no python, no pip).

## What NOT to adopt
* ⛔ **The code.** Unlicensed clone. Any reimplementation is written from the
  mechanism, in our words, in C.
* ⛔ **`curl -skfL`** (insecure). Our relay verifies by default; never ship a
  bootstrap with verification off.
* ⛔ **`--shell` with an arbitrary command.** A fixed, audited entrypoint is
  the requirement.

**Not settled:** whether `curl` exists in a given cage (ours does; not
measured for another).

title: Reference: wiretap — refuse WireGuard/gVisor (needs privileged TUN+UDP); adopt the operator-side SOCKS capability
body:
# Reference: sandialabs/wiretap — refuse the architecture, adopt one capability

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a build
decision.**

**Provenance.** commit `104be99c29e8`, mined 2026-09-28 (route gh, control
reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker: 109 issues+PRs, 155 comments, 114 review comments,
3 discussions. Three passes read. Cite this commit beside every line.

**The refusal, with its measured reason.** wiretap is a WireGuard mesh with a
gVisor userspace stack. Its own `README.md:56`: "**Privileged access
necessary to configure WireGuard interfaces**"; `:66`: "**Bidirectional UDP**
communication between Server and Client on one port". A cage that cannot
`bind(2)` **even at uid 0** (measured) cannot install a WireGuard interface,
inject routes, or rely on UDP. Refused before code. `src/transport/tcp/tcp.go`
is vendored tailscale `netstack` and its dependency is *the interface*, not
the forwarding, so the "experimental TCP" path is not a fallback for us.

## What to adopt
1. **`expose --dynamic`: an operator-side SOCKS5 that reaches a client.**
   `src/cmd/expose.go` (`--dynamic`/`-d`, `--remote`, `--server-address`);
   `src/api/api.go:185 Expose(..., dynamic bool)` plumbs it to the server, so
   it is **implemented** (README:521's "Reverse Socks5 Support" is a
   different, reverse-direction roadmap item). README:478-492: the *servers*
   bind SOCKS5 on the remote port and rewrite the destination, so any client
   can reach the cage. Two properties worth taking: the listener is on the
   operator (the only place it can be), and ⛔ **the server forgets forwards
   on restart** (README:481) — a property to choose deliberately.
   ⛔ Not new: chisel's `socks` remote does the same, and wiretap filed #20
   and #17 for it. File the **capability** against dropssh (`grep -rn socks
   src/` → nothing); it is genuinely missing.

2. **E2EE nested inside a relay the relay cannot read**
   (`src/transport/userspace/UserspaceSocketBind`, adapted from
   wireguard-go). ⛔ **confirms** what we already have, better: our E2EE is
   ssh's, so dropbear is already the server.

## What NOT to adopt
* ⛔ WireGuard as the transport (TUN, privilege, UDP; and wiretap's own #61
  reports it blocked in some jurisdictions).
* ⛔ gVisor `netstack` — it exists to present a routed IP interface; ssh
  gives a byte stream and a login.
* ⛔ The REST control plane (its #20 proposed it, `src/api/api.go` exists). A
  new surface; our honest version is structured events on stderr (R4), not a
  control API.

## Tracker findings, with the numbers
* ⛔ **#16 (closed)**: ~**14 MB rss per TCP connection**, OOM-killed at ~88k
  conns on 2 GB. ⛔ The reporter's `rss` under an nmap/masscan load, not a
  controlled benchmark, 2023-vintage code. A **cost signal about gVisor
  stacks** — the single most useful thing here, and a reason not to adopt the
  stack.
* **#15 (closed)** userspace SYN-SENT exhaustion during scans. Same family.
* **#11 (closed)** a user could not supply two keypairs and wanted the
  pre-0.3 single tunnel back: E2EE layering is a real operational cost its own
  users pushed back on.
* **#22 (closed)** users wanted a PTY shell on the exit node. ⛔ Our cage has
  **no `/dev/ptmx`** (measured) — dead on arrival, recorded so it is not
  re-proposed.

title: Reference: ligolo-ng — adopt agent-dials-out + yamux shape; TUN is on the proxy, not the cage
body:
# Reference: nicocha30/ligolo-ng — adopt the agent-dials-out shape

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a build
decision.**

**Provenance.** commit `e543732f4be6`, mined 2026-09-28 (route gh, control
reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker: 188 issues+PRs, 416 comments, 29 review
comments, 6 discussions. Three passes read. Cite this commit beside every line.

**Why this one matters most.** ligolo is the reference whose *architecture*
fits our cage, for a precise reason: **the TUN is on the proxy (operator) side,
never on the agent.** `pkg/proxy/netstack/stack.go:199-206` opens the TUN
(`tun.New`, `CreateNIC`) in the **proxy**; the **agent**
(`cmd/agent/main.go`) dials out over one websocket with **yamux** multiplexed
on it:

* `:325` `websocket.Dial(...)` (honours an HTTP/SOCKS proxy, `goproxy`);
* `:331` `websocket.NetConn(..., MessageBinary)` — a websocket as a `net.Conn`;
* `:240` `yamux.Server(conn, cfg)` and `:248` `Accept()` — many streams, one
  socket.

That is exactly the problem dropssh's `docs/multiplexing.md` is solving with
hand-rolled 32-hex session ids, and exactly what the ajam relay does with an
id prefix. The cage opens no device, sets no route, and needs no privilege.

## What to adopt
1. **A standard multiplexer with per-stream windows and keepalive.**
   `cmd/agent/main.go:233-238`: `EnableKeepAlive`, 60 s keepalive, 120 s
   `ConnectionWriteTimeout`, **16 MB `MaxStreamWindowSize`**. ⛔ This is an
   **opinion, not a measurement**, and the open question is real: the ajam
   relay imposes its **own** framing (32-hex id on the node leg), so yamux
   would run *inside* an already-framed data channel. Not settled.
2. **A total reconnection budget.** `:59` `--reconnect-timeout 300` (a *total*
   budget, so an agent gives up rather than retrying forever). Our B-list says
   "backoff and jitter, capped" with no total. Adopt the total, make it visible.
3. **Cert-fingerprint pinning** (`--accept-fingerprint`, SHA256, with
   `--ignore-cert` only for debug). Same posture as our token+TLS; right for a
   box with no CA bundle (our R7).

## What NOT to adopt
* ⛔ **The TUN + gVisor netstack on the proxy.** We are a relay, not a router.
* ⛔ **UDP/ICMP framing** (`pkg/relay/relay.go`, 6-byte datagram header).
  Our UDP is unreliable and ssh is TCP.
* ⛔ **The route table / `autoroute`.** A network tool, not a transport.
* ⛔ `--ignore-cert` as a shipped flag.

## Tracker findings the code does not say
* **#101, #65 (closed)** keepalive timeouts — the most-reported class here.
  Same evidence as chisel #608 and our B5, from a third project: **liveness
  and lifecycle, not forwarding, is where this family breaks.**
* **#195 (closed)** "Agent sends no SNI / TLS fails with hostname strings" —
  connect-by-name must send SNI, connect-by-IP cannot. Our DoH→IP→TLS path
  hits this seam; the proxy lesson and the SNI lesson apply together.
* **#127 (closed)** added corporate-proxy support to the agent. On our host
  the relay is reachable *only* through a CONNECT proxy, so this is what made
  the PoC possible.

**Not settled:** whether yamux survives the ajam relay's own framing (above).

title: Reference: chisel — adopt ready/ACL-per-channel, refuse SSH-over-WS
body:
# Reference: jpillora/chisel — adopt 2 mechanisms, refuse the transport

Research unit 2026-09-28 (TEMPLATE methodology). **Evidence, not a build
decision.**

**Provenance.** commit `3c00f04ca154`, mined 2026-09-28 via
`scripts/common/mine-repo.sh` (route gh, control reachable, 0 gaps). Tracker:
607 issues+PRs (both states), 1271 comments, 145 review comments, 0
discussions. Three passes read. Cite this commit beside every line.

**What it is.** Go TCP/UDP tunnel: one SSH connection over a single WebSocket
between client and server, each `remote` an `ssh` channel named `chisel`
(`share/tunnel/tunnel_out_ssh.go`). A `R:` remote inverts which side listens.

**The bindless fact.** The chisel *client* only `net.Listen`s for non-reverse
remotes; the *server* binds for reverse remotes (`server/server_handler.go:142`,
`r.CanListen()` → "Server cannot listen on …"). So cage-as-client in reverse
mode needs no local listener, and its client dials out over one websocket
(`share/cnet/conn_ws.go`).

## What to adopt
1. **`ready`/`reject{id,reason}` handshake with a bounded wait.**
   `server_handler.go:89` (10 s `CONFIG_TIMEOUT`) and the explicit `reject`
   the relay already forwards. Our `serve.c` currently only *logs* `open`.
2. **ACL on every channel, re-read live.** `tunnel_out_ssh.go:53`
   (`t.Config.ACL(hostPort)`) checks each new channel and re-resolves the user
   so an authfile reload applies to connected clients. chisel's own open issue
   **#549** shows a live session is *not* torn down on reload — the gap to
   close, not copy.

## What NOT to adopt
* ⛔ **SSH-over-WebSocket transport.** We already terminate ssh end to end;
  a second SSH layer would make the relay read the session (our `AGENTS.md`:
  the relay carries ciphertext and nothing else).
* ⛔ **Its SOCKS5 server** (`share/tunnel/tunnel.go`). In a cage a SOCKS
  cannot bind; the operator side is where it belongs. A reverse-SOCKS is a
  real dropssh gap but is a dropssh feature, not a chisel import.
* ⛔ **`--auth` user:pass** (weaker than pubkey + token) and the `ck-` key
  format (base64 ECDSA, unencrypted at rest, `ccrypto/keys_helpers.go`).

## Tracker findings the code does not say
* **#608 (open)** goroutine leak + nil panic — but `keepAlivePing` now races
  a timeout and the `r==nil` guard is present at HEAD, so the issue is
  **stale relative to code**. Evidence of intent, not behaviour.
* **#579, #560 (open)** re-listen/reconnect churn after restart and idle
  timeouts. Connection **lifecycle**, not forwarding, is where these break —
  the same class as our B5 and B9.

**Not settled:** whether a chisel client runs in our cage. Plausibly yes
(reverse mode dials out), but chisel was not run.

Deep reviews: the door sweep, guard mutation and claim audit for the whole
sweep are in the corpus; for this reference the claim audit re-opened every
citation above (all resolve). Verdict stands.

title: Research: the gap is the multiplexed reverse path, and B11 is stale (bare frame closes 1009, not silent)
body:
# The gap this sweep found, and a correction to B11

Research unit, 2026-09-28. Method: TEMPLATE `docs/methodology/research.md`.
**This is evidence, not a decision to build.** Full corpus: seven references
read at the commits named in each linked issue. This issue carries the two
things that are about *this* project.

## What was proved, live

A cage that **cannot `bind(2)` even at uid 0**, has **no `/dev/ptmx`**, **no
`/etc/passwd`**, **no resolver**, opens **no direct TCP socket**, and reaches
the world only through an HTTP CONNECT proxy that answers **`200 Connection
Established` on 443 and `403 not on the egress allowlist` on every other
port** (24/24 trials, mutation-proven) **can hold one long-lived websocket to
the reverse relay and speak the multiplexed protocol end to end.**

Live transcript (`poc/10-reverse-relay-multiplex.js`, 3 consecutive runs,
identical):

```
node TEXT  {"type":"hello","version":1,"maxFrameBytes":65536,"maxSessions":64}
node TEXT  {"type":"open","id":"7033d9d..."}
->  node answers open with TEXT {"type":"ready","id":...}
op  TEXT  {"type":"ready","id":"7033d9d..."}
node BIN  "7033d9d...OP-BARE-FRAME"          # operator bare, relay PREPENDS
op  BIN   "NODE-PREFIXED-A"                    # node id+payload, relay STRIPS
op  BIN   "NODE-PREFIXED-B"
```

Every rule in `docs/reverse-relay.md` reproduced. The relay is reachable from
the exact environment dropssh targets, so **B1/B2 are implementation work, not
a reachability unknown.**

## ⛔ Correction: B11 and `reverse-relay.md` are stale on the bare-frame failure

Both say a bare node frame is **silently dropped** — "no error, no close, and
the session goes quiet" — in **five places**:

* `docs/reverse-relay.md:109`
* `docs/relay-issues.md:49` (B2), `:63` (B2 table), `:217` (B11)
* `docs/multiplexing.md:38`

Measured live 2026-09-28, 3/3 runs: a bare node frame closes the node socket
with **code 1009, reason `bad multiplex frame`**, and the operator then sees
1011 `node disconnected`. ⛔ **Close code 1009 appears in none of those five
documents**, and `reverse-relay.md`'s error table lists only `node open
timeout` and `binary frames required`. So an implementer following the docs
has no way to know 1009 exists, which is the code they will actually see.

**The requirement is unchanged** (the node must prefix the 32-hex id). What
changed is the failure is now **loud and named**, so B11's "looks like a relay
that is not working" is wrong. ⛔ We cannot say the relay *changed*: the
document's measurement is from 2026-09-27 and we have no instrumented run from
that day. The honest statement is that the doc and the live relay disagree.

A second close reason, `1003 binary frames required`, **is** in the error
table but is the *first* failure a naive implementer hits (a TEXT frame on the
data leg), and in C the opcode is chosen by the frame writer, so 1003 and
1009 must be logged distinctly.

**Asks:** (1) correct all five places and add 1009 to the error table;
(2) make **R11** assert the *close*, not the silence; (3) the PoC is a working
version of what **R1** asks for and can be ported into `tests/`.

## What the gap is, confirmed in source not docs

Read `src/serve.c:458-476`: `open` is logged and dropped, the first
non-control bytes start one session, and the loop `break`s to redial. That is
**B1, B2 and B5** in twelve lines, and `src/ws.c:726 ws_read` returns from a
single `pending` buffer, which is **B4**. So the multiplexed reverse path is
**specified and not implemented**, and the four transferable mechanisms from
the seven references land inside it:

1. answer every `open` with `ready`/`reject{id,reason}` within a bound
   (chisel `server_handler.go:89`);
2. ACL on every channel, re-read live so a reload applies (chisel
   `share/tunnel/tunnel_out_ssh.go:53`; its own #549 shows the gap);
3. a standard multiplexer with per-stream windows (ligolo
   `cmd/agent/main.go:233-240`, yamux 16 MB window, 60 s keepalive) ⛔ an
   opinion, and the relay's own 32-hex framing would have to carry it;
4. a **total** reconnection budget, visible (ligolo
   `cmd/agent/main.go:59`, `--reconnect-timeout 300`).

**What was NOT established:** no ssh session, no dropbear, one session only
(so B5 is not exercised), one machine one day, and the seven references were
read rather than run. Full scope in the linked findings.

title: sandhome: a portable bootstrap, toolchain home, skills and five review passes
body:
Greetings from Port Edwards. This turns the sandssh checkout into sandhome:
one bootstrap, one environment, and the skills, guides and tools an agent
needs to make a bare userland workable. The problem it exists for is measured,
not assumed — a mount can be writable and still refuse execve, so data and
executables are split across two roots chosen by running a real file.

Added: bootstrap.sh (self-fetching when piped), bin/sandhome, a POSIX-sh
library (detect, space plan, fetch+digest, env, toolchain contract, shims,
report), seven toolchain modules, three Agent Skills, a guide and decision
pages, and CI. `sh tests/run.sh` runs 173 checks green over dash and
bash --posix syntax, the exec split, the mirror, the toolchain framework, the
shims, an end-to-end noexec install, and errandsh over pipes.

Five review passes each fixed a defect with a test that failed before the fix:
the requirements cycle guard and recursion that clobbered the parent;
tr/find/temp-root portability; unquoted paths in generated env files and a
read-at-EOF bug that silently broke version lookup; npm broken by dereferencing
a symlinked executable, and `go run` broken by a build cache on a noexec root;
and a dry-run report claiming shims it never built. Verified against real jq,
npm 11.19.1 and Go 1.27.1.

We aim to provide the software that shapes the world of tomorrow.

---

Requested by Ajam via errand.
